title: DPO explained: no reward model, no RL — one classification loss is all RLHF needs
summary: RLHF requires training a reward model and then optimizing with PPO: powerful but complex and unstable. DPO shows the optimal policy has a closed form; after a change of variables, the reward model cancels out and only a binary classification loss remains. We work through the derivation, compute the optimal policy and DPO loss by hand, then compare experiments with PPO and unpack the problems with using GPT-4 as a judge.
ai_summary: Direct Preference Optimization (Stanford University, 2023) shows that the RLHF objective of maximizing reward minus β times the KL penalty has a closed-form optimum: the reference model reweighted by exp(reward / β). Inverting this, the reward can be written as β · log(π / π_ref) plus a prompt-only constant; substituting into the Bradley-Terry preference model cancels the constant and leaves a binary classification loss that depends only on the language model — no reward model, no reinforcement learning, no sampling during training. On sentiment control, DPO's reward–KL frontier dominates PPO; on summarization, GPT-4 win rate is about 61%, above PPO's 57%; on single-turn dialogue it matches Best of 128. The largest experiments use up to 6 billion parameters.
brief: Problem: RLHF requires training a reward model, optimizing with PPO, and sampling responses during training — complex, expensive, and unstable.

Method: invert the closed-form optimum of the reward-minus-KL objective to express the reward as the log probability ratio between the policy and the reference model, yielding a binary classification loss.
Result: it optimizes the same objective as RLHF; DPO's frontier beats PPO on sentiment control, wins summarization about 61% to 57%, and matches Best of 128 on dialogue.

Limitations: tested only up to 6 billion parameters, relies on offline preference data, and GPT-4 judging is prompt-sensitive; in the reasoning-model era, reinforcement learning is back at center stage.

paper.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
paper.authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn

cover.headline: A close read of the original DPO paper
cover.highlight: Your language model is secretly a reward model

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In May 2023, Stanford's Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher Manning, and Chelsea Finn released this paper, later published at NeurIPS 2023. Its subtitle is provocative: **your language model is secretly a reward model**.

It aims to simplify RLHF, which we covered earlier in this series (see our close read of InstructGPT). RLHF first trains a reward model on human preference data, then uses PPO to push the language model toward high scores while a KL penalty holds it back. The pipeline requires keeping several models in sync and continuously generating responses during training — expensive and unstable.

DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) is built on the insight that the 'optimal model' RLHF is looking for can be written down directly as a mathematical formula. Substitute that formula back into the preference model, and the reward model drops out of the loss function, leaving only the language model itself. The whole of RLHF can then be replaced by a simple classification loss: for each preferred/dispreferred pair, make the model favor the preferred response over the dispreferred one, relative to the reference model. No separate reward model, no reinforcement learning, and no generating responses during training.

Experimentally, DPO balances reward and KL better than PPO on sentiment control. On summarization, GPT-4 judges its win rate at about 61%, above PPO's best 57%. On single-turn dialogue, it is the only computationally cheap method that also beats the dataset's chosen responses. It needs almost no hyperparameter tuning.

callout.title: One-sentence version
callout.text: DPO = write RLHF's optimal policy in closed form + change variables to make the reward model disappear + a binary classification loss: -log σ(β · [log(π / π_{ref})(preferred) - log(π / π_{ref})(dispreferred)]). It optimizes the same objective as RLHF, but works like ordinary fine-tuning of a single model.

callout.title: Four concepts you need before reading
callout.text: If these are unfamiliar, don't worry; these four are enough:
list: **The three RLHF steps**: supervised fine-tuning → train a reward model on human preferences → optimize with reinforcement learning (PPO). See our close read of InstructGPT.
**Bradley-Terry model**: the larger the reward gap between two responses, the more likely a human picks the higher-reward one. That probability is σ(r_{1} - r_{2}).
**KL divergence**: measures how far apart two probability distributions are. RLHF uses it to penalize moving too far from the reference model.
**Reference model π_{ref}**: the model at the start of training, usually the supervised-fine-tuned one. It is held fixed during training.

sections.h: The problem: RLHF works, but it's too complicated

blocks.p: The paper opens by explaining why preference learning matters. Large models are trained on vast amounts of human-written data, produced by people with very different goals and skill levels. We might want a coding assistant to understand common bugs so it can correct them, but to favor rare high-quality code when writing its own; we might want a model to know about a misconception that 50% of people believe, but never to state it as fact in 50% of its answers. **Selecting the behaviors we want from the model's broad knowledge** is key to making AI safe, useful, and controllable.

RLHF was the most successful approach at the time, but the pipeline is far more complicated than supervised learning: it requires training multiple language models (policy, reward model, value function, plus a reference model) and constantly sampling responses from the policy inside the training loop. This is computationally expensive, and PPO is notoriously unstable and hyperparameter-sensitive.

blocks.p: First, let's write RLHF out clearly. Preference data is labeled by humans: given a prompt x and two responses, they prefer y_{w} (w for win) over y_{l} (l for lose). Assume there is a hidden 'true reward' r^{*} in each human's mind, and choices follow the Bradley-Terry model:

parts.desc: Probability that a human considers y_{1} better than y_{2}
The sigmoid function, which turns a reward difference into a probability between 0 and 1

plain.title: Like chess ratings
plain.text: Two responses are like two chess players, each with a hidden rating (the reward). The chance of winning depends only on the rating gap: a gap of 0 gives a 50-50 chance; a gap of 2 means the higher-rated player wins about nine times in ten. σ is the S-shaped curve that turns rating gap into win probability.

blocks.p: **Step one: train a reward model r_{φ}.** Make it assign higher scores to human-chosen responses. The loss is -log σ(r_{φ}(x, y_{w}) - r_{φ}(x, y_{l})), exactly the reward-model loss in InstructGPT.
**Step two: reinforcement learning.** Let the language model π_{θ} generate high-reward responses, but not drift too far from the reference model π_{ref}:

formula.expr: max_{π_{θ}} E_{x∼D, y∼π_{θ}(y|x)} [ r_{φ}(x, y) ] − β · D_{KL}[ π_{θ}(y | x) ‖ π_{ref}(y | x) ]

parts.desc: The average reward earned by responses the model generates
How far the model's distribution is from the reference model. This 'leash' stops the model from gaming the reward model and preserves response diversity.
How tight the leash is: larger β means the model may deviate less from the reference model

formula.note: Language is discrete, so this objective cannot be differentiated directly. RLHF therefore needs reinforcement-learning algorithms such as PPO. That is the source of the complexity and instability.

plain.title: Chasing reward, but on a leash
plain.text: The language model is like a dog; the reward is a star ahead it wants to run toward, and the reference model is the handler holding the leash. β · KL is the leash: the farther the model runs from the reference model, the harder it is pulled back. A larger β is a shorter leash — the model is less willing to wander.

sections.h: The key step: the optimal model can be written down directly

blocks.p: The paper starts from a long-known result: for the objective above — maximizing reward minus KL — the **optimum has a closed form** (derived in Appendix A.1):

formula.expr: π_{r}(y | x) = (1 / Z(x)) · π_{ref}(y | x) · exp( r(x, y) / β )

parts.desc: The probability the reference model originally assigned to this response
A reward-based amplification factor: the higher the reward, the more it is amplified
Partition function: sums over all possible responses so probabilities add to 1. It requires summing over every possible response, so it cannot actually be computed.
The scaling 'temperature': a small β amplifies the reward's influence and makes the model greedier; a large β keeps it closer to the reference model

plain.title: Reweighting the original preferences by reward
plain.text: The reference model has its own prior preference among three responses (gray). The optimal model does something simple: multiply each response by a factor e^(r/β) that grows with reward, then rescale everything to sum to 1. High-reward responses are pushed up and low-reward ones pushed down (green).

callout.title: Optimal model = reference model reweighted by reward
callout.text: Think of it this way: the reference model has its own 'tastes', and the optimal model multiplies each response by a reward-based factor before renormalizing. Good responses become more likely, bad ones less likely, but the model never invents responses the reference model would never produce. β controls how aggressively the probabilities are pushed up and down.

fig.title: Working through the optimal model: same rewards, smaller β is greedier
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: three candidate responses with made-up reference probabilities and rewards; computed from π ∝ π_{ref} · exp(r / β).
fig.note: Response C has the highest reward, yet the reference model gives it only 0.2 probability. With β = 0.5 the optimal model raises it to 0.80; with β = 5 it rises only to 0.26, almost indistinguishable from the reference model.

blocks.p: The formula on its own isn't directly usable because Z(x) cannot be computed. DPO's insight is to **use it in reverse**: take logs on both sides, rearrange, and write the reward in terms of the optimal model:

formula.expr: r(x, y) = β · log[ π_{r}(y | x) / π_{ref}(y | x) ] + β · log Z(x)

parts.desc: How much more the optimal model prefers this response over the reference model (logged, then multiplied by β)
A term that depends only on the prompt x and not on the response y

formula.note: This step reverses the mapping from reward to optimal model: every reward function corresponds to an optimal model, and conversely a model defines a reward.

plain.title: Read in reverse: what a model prefers reveals what it scores highly
plain.text: Since 'optimal model = reference model × reward factor', we can read it backward: look at which response the optimal model prefers over the reference model, and by how much, and we can read off the reward inside it. There is no need to train a separate reward model; the reward is hidden in the probability ratio of the two models.

sections.h: Change of variables: the reward model disappears from the loss

blocks.p: Here is the crucial step. The Bradley-Terry model only cares about the **reward difference between two responses**. Substitute the expression above, and the impossible β · log Z(x) term cancels when the two responses are subtracted. The human preference probability then depends only on the optimal model and the reference model.
So we can fit a parameterized language model π_{θ} to the preference data by maximum likelihood, just as we would train a reward model. That yields the DPO loss:

formula.expr: L_{DPO}(π_{θ}; π_{ref}) = - E_{(x, y_{w}, y_{l})∼D} [ log σ( β · log( π_{θ}(y_{w}|x) / π_{ref}(y_{w}|x) ) - β · log( π_{θ}(y_{l}|x) / π_{ref}(y_{l}|x) ) ) ]

parts.desc: The paper calls this the language model's **implicit reward** r̂_{θ}: how much more the model prefers this response over the reference model.
The difference in implicit reward between the preferred and dispreferred responses
Exactly the same shape as the reward-model loss: the larger the difference, the lower the loss.

formula.note: Compare the two: the reward-model loss is -log σ(r_{φ}(y_{w}) - r_{φ}(y_{l})); DPO simply replaces r_{φ} with β · log(π_{θ} / π_{ref}). That is the subtitle's meaning: **your language model is secretly a reward model**.

plain.title: No judge: compare pairs directly
plain.text: RLHF first trains a judge (the reward model) to score responses, then has the model chase those scores. DPO skips the judge: for each pair of responses, it pushes up the probability of the human-chosen one (y_w) and pushes down the rejected one (y_l), all relative to the reference model. The whole process becomes an ordinary classification loss.

blocks.p: The PyTorch implementation in the paper's appendix is only a few lines: compute the policy's and reference model's log probabilities for the preferred and dispreferred responses, take the difference, multiply by β, and take the negative log sigmoid.

fig.title: Working through the DPO loss: correct rankings cost little, reversed rankings cost a lot — and carry a larger gradient weight
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers made up by us. β = 0.1; 'log ratio' means log π_{θ} - log π_{ref}, or how much more the model prefers a response over the reference model.
columns: Implicit reward difference β × (difference between the two)
rows: Ranked right, but only a little
Ranked wrong: the dispreferred response is pushed higher
fig.note: The gradient weight decides how hard each pair pushes the model. Pairs that are already ranked correctly barely push at all; reversed pairs push the hardest. This is why DPO doesn't 'overshoot'.

quiz.q: In DPO's derivation, how does the uncomputable partition function Z(x) disappear?
options: The Bradley-Terry model only looks at the reward difference between two responses, and β log Z(x) depends only on the prompt, so subtracting the two responses cancels it.
It is estimated by Monte Carlo sampling.
It is absorbed into the value function.
quiz.why: When comparing two responses under the same prompt x, β log Z(x) is identical for both, so subtraction removes it. This is the key that makes DPO possible: it sidesteps the most difficult term to compute in RLHF.

sections.h: What the DPO update actually does

blocks.p: The gradient makes this clearest. The gradient of the DPO loss with respect to the model parameters can be written as:

parts.desc: Increase the probability of the preferred response
Decrease the probability of the dispreferred response
Per-example weight: the more wrong the implicit reward model's ranking of the pair — i.e., the dispreferred response scores higher — the larger the weight

plain.title: A teacher only spends time on the problems you got wrong
plain.text: The σ in front of the gradient is 'how wrong this example is.' When the model already ranks the preferred response above the dispreferred one (left), σ is small and it only nudges. When the ranking is reversed (right), σ is close to 1 and it corrects hard. The paper says removing this weight and pushing every pair equally causes the model to degenerate.

blocks.p: Intuitively, the rule is simple: **increase the probability of the preferred response and decrease that of the dispreferred one.** The weight is the key. Samples the model already ranks correctly have a tiny weight and barely update it; samples that are misranked have a large weight. The paper says that if you drop this weight and simply push preferred responses up and dispreferred ones down, the language model degenerates. The appendix shows summaries from Unlikelihood, a method that does exactly this, full of repeated 'when when when'.

callout.title: "DPO doesn't need a reward model, so it's a different thing from RLHF"
callout.text: DPO has no **explicit** reward model, but it optimizes exactly the same objective as RLHF: maximize reward minus β times the KL divergence. It simply changes the parameterization, making the reward implicit in the probability ratio between the policy and the reference model. DPO is therefore just as constrained by preference-data quality as RLHF, and just as susceptible to over-optimization.

blocks.p: **How to choose the reference model.** Preference data is usually generated with some supervised fine-tuned model, and DPO uses that model as π_{ref}. If that model is unavailable (for example, when you use a public preference dataset directly), the paper's approach is to first run maximum-likelihood fine-tuning on the preferred responses to obtain a reference model, reducing distribution mismatch.

sections.h: Theory: why this loses no generality

blocks.p: A natural question: does restricting the reward to the form β · log(π / π_{ref}) miss some reward functions? Section 5.1 of the paper answers this.

list: **Equivalence class.** Two reward functions are equivalent if they differ only by a function that depends on the prompt x.

**Lemma 1.** Reward functions in the same equivalence class produce exactly the same preference distribution under the Bradley-Terry model (and the more general Plackett-Luce model). This also means preference data alone can never distinguish them in the first place.
**Lemma 2.** Reward functions in the same equivalence class yield the same optimal policy under the KL-constrained reinforcement learning problem.
**Theorem 1.** Under mild assumptions, every equivalence class can be represented in the form β · log(π / π_{ref}). So DPO's parameterization does not throw away anything that could be learned.

plain.title: Scoring rubrics that differ by a constant count as the same
plain.text: Two teachers grade every question on the same exam, and one always gives 5 more points than the other. When you compare which paper is better, that fixed offset cancels out; the two grading scales are indistinguishable. The paper proves that any two reward functions differing only by a prompt-dependent constant yield the same preferences and the same optimal policy, so DPO's form misses nothing.

blocks.p: The paper also uses this framework to explain why PPO is unstable: the objective RLHF actually optimizes contains a normalization term involving Z(x), which acts as a "soft value function" for the reference model. It does not affect the optimum, but without it the variance of the policy gradient can be large. PPO either learns a value function to estimate it or uses human-written responses as a rough baseline; DPO's parameterization naturally needs no baseline at all.

quiz.q: The paper says that reward functions in the same equivalence class produce the same preference distribution. What does that mean?
options: Preference data can uniquely determine the reward function
Two reward functions that differ only by a constant independent of the response are indistinguishable from preference data; DPO only needs to learn either one.
quiz.why: Because preferences depend only on reward differences, adding the same number to all responses under a prompt changes neither preferences nor the optimal policy. So learning either one is fine. DPO happens to choose the one that keeps the optimal policy automatically normalized.

sections.h: Experiments: three tasks, up to 6 billion parameters

fig.title: Three tasks, three base models
fig.subtitle: Compiled from Section 6 of the paper
rows: IMDb movie review openings; preferences generated by a sentiment classifier (more positive is preferred)
True reward is available, so reward–KL curves can be drawn
Reddit TL;DR posts; human preferences from Stiennon et al.
GPT-4 judging, compared with human-written summaries from the test set
Anthropic Helpful and Harmless dialogue dataset, about 170,000 conversations
GPT-4 judging, compared with the preferred responses in the test set

blocks.p: Baselines include: GPT-J zero-shot, Pythia-2.8B with two-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), fine-tuning only on preferred responses (Preferred-FT), Unlikelihood, PPO (with the learned reward), PPO-GT (uses the true reward directly, as an upper-bound reference), and Best of N (sample N responses from the SFT model and use the reward model to pick the best; it works well but requires generating N times at inference, which is costly).

**Result one: DPO spends KL better.** On the sentiment task, the true reward is known, so one can directly compare who gets more reward at the same KL. The paper ran 22 experiments with different hyperparameters, and DPO's reward–KL frontier was the highest at every KL level. DPO and PPO optimize the same objective, yet DPO strictly dominates; it even beats PPO-GT, which can use the true reward directly.

**Result two: summarization.** GPT-4 win rate against human-written summaries in the test set: DPO at temperature 0 is about 61%, above PPO's 57% at its best temperature, also 0, and above Best of N's best result. DPO is also much more robust to sampling temperature; at high temperatures PPO degrades to the level of the base GPT-J. The paper notes that DPO's β was barely tuned, so these results may understate it.

**Result three: single-turn dialogue.** DPO is the only computationally cheap method that also beats the preferred responses in the dataset, and it is on par with Best of 128, which requires sampling 128 responses. The paper also tried a well-known PPO model trained on the same dataset, but could find no prompt or temperature that made it beat the base Pythia-2.8B.

fig.title: On a different distribution: DPO still clearly beats PPO on news summarization
fig.subtitle: GPT-4-judged win rates against human-written CNN / DailyMail summaries, from Table 1 of the paper. The model was trained on Reddit posts. Blue columns are temperature 0.
fig.note: The paper sees this as preliminary evidence that DPO generalizes no worse than PPO, even though PPO also used unlabeled Reddit prompts.

blocks.p: Training hyperparameters (Appendix B): default β = 0.1 (0.5 for summarization), batch size 64, RMSprop optimizer, learning rate 10^{-6}, linear warmup for the first 150 steps.

The main summarization and dialogue results rely on GPT-4 judgments. To validate this, the paper ran a small human evaluation comparing whether GPT-4 agreed with humans. They found that with a simple prompt asking only which summary better captures the important information, **GPT-4 preferred longer, more verbose summaries**; so they wrote a second prompt that also asked it to consider conciseness, and used the latter for the main results.

fig.title: GPT-4 agrees with humans about as often as humans agree with each other
fig.subtitle: TL;DR summaries; each column compares against PPO at temperature 0, from Table 2 of the paper. Units: %. Amber marks human-human agreement.
rows: Win rate judged by GPT-4 (simple prompt)
Win rate judged by GPT-4 (prompt asking for conciseness)
fig.note: In the DPO column, humans agree with each other only 65% of the time, and GPT-4's agreement with humans is slightly higher. The paper takes this as evidence that GPT-4 is a reasonable substitute for human evaluation.

callout.title: Read these conclusions with caution
callout.text: The human evaluation is small and was only done for summarization. The paper itself notes in its limitations that GPT-4's win rates are prompt-sensitive, and that producing high-quality judgments from automatic evaluators still needs research. Using large models as judges later became widespread, and their bias toward longer answers has been found repeatedly.

list: **The "removing the weight causes degeneration" example actually comes from a different method.** Section 4 says that removing the gradient weight causes degeneration and points to Appendix Table 3; but Table 3 shows summaries generated by Unlikelihood, which is similar to DPO without the weight but not exactly the same thing.
**A small citation error in the formulas.** Section 5.2 says π^{*} is the optimal policy derived from Equation 7, but Equation 7 is the DPO loss; the closed-form optimal policy is Equation 4.

**Limited scale.** Summarization uses the 6B-parameter GPT-J, and dialogue uses the 2.8B-parameter Pythia. The paper explicitly lists scaling to frontier models several orders of magnitude larger as future work.
**No fair PPO baseline for dialogue.** The paper could not find a PPO model that behaved properly, so it used Best of 128 as a rough stand-in for PPO-level performance.

blocks.p: The paper's own open questions:

list: **Generalization.** How does DPO perform out of distribution compared with training with an explicit reward model? Preliminary results are comparable, but more comprehensive study is needed. PPO can use unlabeled prompts; can DPO do the same through self-labeling?
**Over-optimization.** In direct preference optimization, what form does reward over-optimization take? The slight dip late in training on the right side of Figure 3 may be exactly that.
**Scale.** Validated only up to 6 billion parameters.
**Evaluation.** GPT-4's judgments are prompt-sensitive.

blocks.p: **What happened next.** DPO is simple, stable, and resource-efficient, so it quickly became the open-source community's default for preference alignment. Meta's Llama 3 also used DPO in its post-training stage. Many variants followed, attempting to fix its overfitting, length bias, and similar problems.

But reinforcement learning did not leave the stage. The next article, the last in this first main line, DeepSeek-R1 (2025), brought reinforcement learning back to center stage. What trains reasoning there is not human preferences but rewards that can be automatically checked, such as whether a math answer is correct. At that point the model needs to keep trying and generate new solution traces during training, which is exactly what offline-data-only methods like DPO cannot do.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

options: β · log(π_{θ}(y | x) / π_{ref}(y | x)): how much more the model prefers this response over the reference model
quiz.why: This is DPO's core change of variables: the log probability ratio between the policy and the reference model, multiplied by β, is a valid reward function, up to a prompt-only constant, which does not affect preferences or the optimal policy.

quiz.q: If you make DPO's β very large, what happens to the trained model?
options: It leans toward preferred responses more aggressively.
It stays closer to the reference model, with little change.
quiz.why: β corresponds to the KL penalty strength in RLHF. The larger β is, the closer the optimal policy stays to the reference model, as in the β = 5 column of the hand-computed table. Smaller β chases the preference more greedily, but also overfits the preference data more easily.

blocks.p: After reading, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What is RLHF's objective function? Why is reinforcement learning used to optimize it?
What does the optimal policy of the reward-minus-KL objective look like? What role does β play?
How does DPO express reward in terms of the model? Why does Z(x) cancel out?
How is the DPO loss similar to the reward-model loss, and how is it different?
Why is the weight in DPO's gradient important?
Why is DPO's parameterization said to lose no generality?
In the three experiments, what does DPO compare against, and where does it win?
What problems arise when using GPT-4 as a judge? How does the paper validate it?
